title: Night buses
text: A city transport agency added late-night buses to one route and counted more passengers after midnight. At the same time, it moved the route’s first stop to the main exit of a hospital. The agency interpreted the increase as evidence that a shortage of departures had kept hospital workers from using the bus. However, some workers may instead have been deterred by the walk to the old stop. A trial that varies departure frequency and stop location independently would help the agency decide which change to keep.

title: Ink on reused paper
text: An archive labels a collection of merchants’ notes as informal, partly because entries are written on the reverse of older letters. But an examination of surviving stationery from the same period shows that many formal bills also reused sheets. Paper was expensive, and reuse was widespread among offices. The physical support alone is therefore a weak guide to an entry’s function. Recurring signatures and evidence that balances were carried to a systematic ledger would be more informative.

title: Bird surveys
text: Two surveys reported fewer meadow birds after a path was widened. Both surveyed the path at dawn, but the earlier survey began late in spring while the later survey began several weeks earlier. During the earlier weeks, some species sing less often because they have not yet established territories. The apparent decline might therefore reflect a change in how easily the birds were noticed. Repeating both surveys at the same dates would reduce that uncertainty, although it would leave open whether weather or habitat also changed.

title: Repairable instruments
text: A laboratory replaced its custom instruments with a standard model after predicting that repairs would become faster. For the first year average repair times rose. Some managers wanted to reverse the purchase, but the technician noted that spare parts for the standard model were still arriving through the temporary purchasing process. Once stock was on hand, technicians could swap a module without fabricating a replacement. The first year measured how repair worked during a transition whose main constraint was supply.

title: An exhibition in two rooms
text: A museum displayed early sketches in one room and the finished paintings in another. A reviewer called the arrangement a chronological display. Yet the dates of several finished paintings precede dates written on drawings, because the artist returned to some subjects after exhibiting them. The layout is better understood as a comparison of working methods. Visitors can follow the repeated image of a bridge across ink, charcoal, and canvas even when the surviving dates resist a linear narrative.

title: A cooler roof
text: A school painted one building’s roof white and recorded lower afternoon temperatures on the top floor. The average across all floors hardly moved. An article cited the building average as evidence that the paint did little to improve conditions for students. But students on the upper floor had previously reported the most heat discomfort and accounted for almost all of the complaints. The building average hides which rooms were affected and how those rooms relate to the problem the school wanted to solve.

title: Markets and seeds
text: A historian argues that a district began growing a new crop because merchants first offered reliable purchase contracts. The earliest surviving contracts are dated three years after letters in which farmers sought seed for that crop. In response, the historian notes that contracts may have circulated before the earliest copies now in the archive. That is possible, but the surviving letters also suggest that farmers wanted a crop that could tolerate declining rainfall. Without evidence of earlier agreements, the contracts are more clearly evidence of commercial expansion than of the first decision to plant.

title: Return visits
text: A survey of a science center found that members returned more often than guests who bought day tickets. Staff concluded that membership encourages repeated visits. Yet the center offered membership at the exit, after visitors had already decided whether they enjoyed the exhibits. People who intended to return could be particularly likely to buy membership. A follow-up offered randomly selected visitors a free trial before their first visit and compared their later visits with the rest of the visitors.

title: Salt-tolerant barley
text: Agronomists tested a salt-tolerant barley variety in coastal fields and recorded higher grain yields than nearby plots planted with a standard strain. A trade bulletin recommended replacing the standard strain across the entire valley. However, the coastal trial plots had high soil salinity, whereas inland farms rely on freshwater irrigation where the standard strain matures ten days earlier and avoids autumn storms. A variety that outperforms under stress does not necessarily dominate where that stress is absent.

title: Dating clay kilns
text: Archaeologists often estimate a settlement's age from pottery styles found in its trash pits. At one hillside site, however, vessels of an older regional style appeared beside iron tools dated two centuries later. Rather than discarding the iron dates, investigators examined the clay chemistry and discovered that local potters had continued using the same mountain quarry and decorative stamps for generations after neighboring towns changed fashions. Stylistic conservatism can make an active workshop look older than it is.

title: Open-plan study halls
text: A university remodeled its library into an open-plan hall after a student poll showed strong demand for collaborative space. One term later, occupancy counts rose during exam weeks, yet complaints about background noise tripled. Staff noticed that quiet booths along the perimeter filled first each morning while large group tables remained half empty until afternoon. Measuring total occupancy alone masked a mismatch between the quiet seating students used most and the collaborative tables the remodel prioritized.

title: Acoustic buoys and whales
text: Shipping lanes near a harbor were shifted southward after acoustic buoys detected fewer whale calls along the southern route. Two years later, aerial surveys spotted similar numbers of whales in both corridors. Marine biologists realized that whales feeding in the southern corridor spent more time diving silently for bottom prey, whereas whales traveling through the northern lane called frequently to stay in contact. Relying on sound detections without visual counts had confused vocal behavior with habitat absence.
